analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada, Europe, and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Health and Human Services Department to write rules letting American pharmacies, wholesalers, and individual consumers import prescription drugs from Canada, the European Union, and other countries with strong drug-safety systems. It would have barred drug makers from punishing sellers who import — for example by cutting off their supply or raising their prices — and made it legal to sell in the U.S. a patented drug first sold abroad by the patent holder. It paired importation with safety rules: counterfeit-resistant packaging, registration and inspections of foreign exporters, and a public list of approved sellers.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and people paying out of pocket, would pay prices closer to what consumers in Canada and Europe pay. The bill's own findings say Americans pay up to 1,000% more for the same drugs and estimate open importation could save consumers at least $635 billion over ten years. Pharmacies, wholesalers, and internet pharmacies would gain a new business importing and selling qualifying drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Pharmacists, pharmacies, and wholesalers could import qualifying drugs from Australia, Canada, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, South Africa, and the EU member countries, with HHS required to write the rules within 180 days.
Individuals could personally import up to a 90-day supply of a qualifying drug from a licensed or registered internet pharmacy with a valid prescription.

Drug makers would be barred from discriminating against importers, including charging them higher prices, denying or delaying supplies, or altering the U.S. version of a drug specifically to block importation, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement including triple damages.
Selling or importing a patented drug first sold abroad under the patent owner's authority would no longer count as patent infringement, opening the door to lower-priced versions of the same drug.
The bill's findings state Americans pay up to 1,000% more than consumers in other countries and estimate importation could save consumers at least $635 billion.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose ability to charge much higher U.S. prices than they charge in Canada and Europe would be undercut. Exporters would pay annual registration fees capped at 1% of their export volume, and drug makers would bear the cost of adding counterfeit-resistant packaging to all prescription drugs sold in the U.S.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs would carry some safety risk even with safeguards: the bill excludes biologics, refrigerated drugs, and controlled substances, but a longer supply chain across borders is harder to police than the current closed U.S. distribution system, and the counterfeit-resistant packaging mandate applies to all prescription drugs, adding packaging costs industry would likely pass on.

The bill depends heavily on HHS and FTC enforcement to work: if foreign exporters are slow to register or manufacturers find legal ways around the anti-discrimination rules, the promised savings could be much smaller than the bill's $635 billion estimate, which came from the bill's own findings rather than an outside analysis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is very large and the bill is unusually detailed about safety — registration, surprise inspections, counterfeit-resistant packaging, a public list of approved sellers, and exclusions for the riskiest drug types. The main honest concerns are enforcement burden and residual supply-chain risk, plus the packaging costs. On balance it was a serious attempt to let Americans buy the same drugs at other countries' prices, and the drawbacks are modest next to the potential savings.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 10, 2007, joined by Sen. Jim DeMint, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote — after the referral on the day of introduction.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Republicans, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without the bill ever advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, so nothing disturbed the practice of charging U.S. patients far higher prices than patients in Canada and Europe pay for the same drugs. American consumers saved nothing.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pharmaceutical Market Access Act of 2007 to legalize drug importation from approved countries.

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senator joined.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
against.what_they_did: The prescription drug industry has consistently opposed importation legislation, citing safety risks and the threat to its U.S. pricing structure.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republicans sponsored the bill and it was referred to a Democratic-chaired committee that never acted; because no votes were ever held, the record shows no partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would break the industry's ability to charge Americans far more for the same drugs sold abroad: parallel importation, a ban on price discrimination and supply cutoffs against importers, and a patent exception for drugs first sold overseas all attack the U.S.-versus-abroad price gap directly. Its gain is consumers' loss — lower drug prices come straight out of manufacturer revenue.

industries.industry: Internet pharmacies, pharmacies, and drug wholesalers
industries.note: The bill creates a legal importation business for pharmacies and wholesalers, including registered internet pharmacies, who would earn margins selling lower-priced foreign drugs. Their interest runs with consumers', who get cheaper drugs through them.

The bill mandates counterfeit-resistant packaging — optically variable features like those on U.S. currency — on all prescription drugs, creating a mandated market for security packaging suppliers. The cost is passed into drug prices, but the aim is protecting buyers from fakes.
